lessons.title: Request, one-shot, and next eligible pulse
lessons.physicalIntuition: A feedback condition requests energy. An accepted request starts a one-shot; the high side stays on for the commanded/clamped duration, then off-time continues until both feedback and eligibility permit another pulse.
lessons.mathematicalDerivation: For an ideal basic COT buck near steady CCM, average fs ≈ D/ton ≈ Vo/(Vin ton), not an exact instantaneous constant. Add clamps ton,min ≤ ton,law ≤ ton,max and enforce toff ≥ toff,min; derive a simple timing-limited duty bound only for uninterrupted repeating pulses.
lessons.modelingConsequence: Represent request, grant, one-shot state, turn-off, off-time lockout, and next eligibility as distinct events. Log denied/delayed triggers and never infer them from a duty ratio alone.
assumptions: ideal steady approximation for average frequency
no skipped pulses or extra scheduler delay in simple duty bound
lessons.transferQuestion: At fixed ton, why does raising Vin usually change average frequency unless the on-time law adapts?

lessons.title: Natural, injected, and emulated ripple
lessons.physicalIntuition: The comparator needs a repeatable crossing with the correct timing slope. That crossing may come from output ESR, an inductor/DCR-derived waveform, an internal ramp, or their sum.
lessons.mathematicalDerivation: Propagate each ripple source through its coupling network to the comparator, compare amplitude/slope to hysteresis, noise, and delay, and identify the phase of the crossing relative to the switching state. Ripple transfer paths can add poles and zeros.
lessons.modelingConsequence: Expose natural and injected signals separately, including source, amplitude, phase/delay, and coupling. Never equate feedback ripple with output ripple or silently add an ideal ramp.
assumptions: linear small-ripple coupling where frequency-domain formulas are used
lessons.transferQuestion: How can ample injected-ripple amplitude still produce poor timing if its phase is wrong?

lessons.title: Delay, hysteresis, noise, and irregular operation
lessons.physicalIntuition: Noise moves a threshold crossing, delay moves the resulting switch transition, and hysteresis changes the next threshold. When feedback slope is shallow, small disturbances become large timing errors.
lessons.mathematicalDerivation: Approximate timing jitter as Delta t ≈ Delta v/noise-to-crossing-slope for small perturbations, then distinguish physical delay from event quantization. The approximation fails with multiple crossings, large noise, saturation, or mode changes.
lessons.modelingConsequence: Use deterministic seeded noise and explicit delay state. The web lab detects crossings on its disclosed integration grid and warns when that resolution is too coarse; a production/PSpice implementation should add event interpolation or tighter event scheduling before attributing jitter to physics.
assumptions: local monotonic crossing for jitter estimate
lessons.transferQuestion: If halving the timestep halves observed jitter, what hypothesis should you test before blaming comparator noise?

lessons.title: Light load, skipping, diode emulation, and protection
lessons.physicalIntuition: At light load, one minimum pulse may deliver too much energy, so controllers skip, burst, or prevent reverse current. During current limit/startup, different comparators or timers can override normal requests.
lessons.mathematicalDerivation: Compare minimum pulse energy/current change with load demand; enforce zero-current turnoff for diode emulation and priority ordering among current limit, min-times, and startup clamps.
lessons.modelingConsequence: Mode transitions are explicit state-machine branches with visible priority. The current web COT pulse and ripple-injection models use a disclosed unidirectional diode-emulation clamp at zero inductor current; they do not demonstrate forced-synchronous negative current. Switching-frequency statistics must state whether skipped intervals are included.
assumptions: behavior is selected educational policy, not universal COT
lessons.transferQuestion: Why can forced CCM show negative current where diode-emulation mode shows a zero-current interval?

lessons.title: Servo loops, error amplifiers, and COT stability
lessons.physicalIntuition: A fast ripple comparator can time pulses while a slower error/servo path corrects DC offset or adjusts a threshold. Even without an external COMP pin, plant, ripple path, delay, and internal loops shape response.
lessons.mathematicalDerivation: Factor a disclosed COT small-signal loop into plant, divider, comparator/ripple dynamics, fixed-on-time delay, and servo where present. Identify conditions such as small ripple, fixed mode, and frequency below switching.
lessons.modelingConsequence: The lesson taxonomy and PSpice block puzzle identify fast ripple and slower servo paths. The current web COT pulse lab models one generic comparator/one-shot path, not a selectable commercial servo architecture; statements such as 'no error amplifier' or 'no compensation' remain architecture-qualified.
lessons.interaction: Guided COT loop-block analysis followed by the PSpice block-construction puzzle
lessons.transferQuestion: How can a controller be marketed as externally compensation-free while still having a shaped loop response?
